newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Rwandan refugees abandon six camps in Tanzania.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan refugees abandon six camps in Tanzania.

text.p: At least 400,000 Rwandan refugees have abandoned their camps in northwestern Tanzania, voting with their feet against a plan to repatriate them by the end of the year, U.N. officials said on Thursday.

On the other side of Rwanda in Zaire, where up to half a million other Rwandan refugees may be adrift in equatorial forests, Zairean rebels declared a unilateral ceasefire in their campaign to overthrow the government in Kinshasa.
In Benaco refugee camp in Tanzania, once the largest in the country with 160,000 to 180,000 Rwandans, only a few stragglers lingered in the debris on Thursday afternoon.

The rest of the refugees disappeared into the distance like ants on the march -- old men, children and even the maim, loaded with mattresses, their other meagre possessions and blue plastic sheeting from their huts in the camp.
"I'm leaving because some of the refugees repatriated yesterday were killed in Rwanda. I'm sure if I go back I will be killed also," said a refugee who gave his name as Theoneste.
The U.N. officials said the five other camps in the area were also deserted, giving a total of between 400,000 and 500,000 people on the loose in the Tanzanian bush.
The exodus started on a small scale last Sunday and began to snowball as word spread through the camps that refugees in other areas had struck camp and headed into the bush.

Members of the Hutu militia, the Interahamwe, do not want to go home for fear of prosecution or reprisals for the massacre of Rwandan Tutsis in 1994. They want the other refugees to stay with them on the grounds there is strength in numbers.
UNHCR had hoped it and the Tanzanians could persuade the refugees to go home willingly, following the example of more than 600,000 who have gone home from Zaire since mid-November.
Instead the plan seems to have backfired. It may end in bands of Rwandan refugees wandering across the Tanzanian bush, just as others are in the forests of Zaire.
"This is not one of the scenarios that was in our plan," said an UNHCR official, staring in disbelief as the Benaco refugees streamed off.
Aid workers quoted refugees as saying they decided to leave when they heard that the Tanzanian military and a delegation from the Rwandan army had passed by Benaco.
The Rwandan military team was on its way to the town of Ngara to coordinate with the Tanzanians on the repatriation but the sight of them put the refugees in a panic, they said.
There was no sign on Thursday that the Tanzanian army was taking any action to prevent the exodus, though some 10,000 Tanzanian troops are posted in the border area.
Earlier on Thursday aid workers quoted refugees as saying they planned to go to Malawi, Zambia, Kenya or Uganda.
About 15,000 refugees fled earlier in the week from camps close to the Ugandan border. About 560 of them crossed the Kigera river by canoe to reach Uganda on the other side.
The Rwandan refugees in Zaire abandoned their camps in October after the Zairean rebel movement, backed by the Rwandan army, went to war against the Zairean government.
The rebels, many of them Zaireans of Rwandan Tutsi origin, have seized a string of towns and villages close to Zaire's eastern borders but their campaign seems to have lost momentum.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila, chairman of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, told Reuters in the border town of Goma on Thursday: "Because of much pressure from abroad we have stopped (the war)."
He said that as part of the ceasefire the advancing rebels had stopped short of the towns of Walikale, west of Goma, and Bunia, north of Goma on the Ugandan border.

"We want them (Kinshasa) to negotiate instead of calling in friends and mercenaries," he added. "This (war) can continue if there is not a clear indication from the international community and the gang in power in Kinshasa to say they are willing to surrender or to start negotiations."
The rebels have declared a unilateral ceasefire before but the Zairean government has previously rejected negotiations.
